scenes.title: AI code review for GitHub Enterprise Server
scenes.sub: A real pull request, reviewed by Microsoft Foundry through MCP, entirely on private networks.
scenes.narration: Hi, and welcome. GitHub Enterprise Server doesn't come with Copilot code review, but many teams that run it still want an AI reviewer on every pull request. In the next few minutes I'll show you one working on a real pull request, and how you can set up the same thing on your own server.

scenes.title: Build the review loop from pieces you already trust
scenes.sub: Your server, your runners, your network, your model deployment.
steps: A developer opens a pull request on GHES, as usual.
GitHub Actions starts a review job on a private runner.
MCP servers give the model your repository and your engineering rules.
Comments on the changed lines and a required status check.
scenes.narration: The idea is simple. When a developer opens a pull request, a GitHub Actions workflow starts a review job on a private runner. The reviewer reads the diff, asks MCP servers for context and for your own engineering rules, calls a model in Microsoft Foundry, and posts the result back as comments and a status check.

scenes.title: Three regions, one private path
bullets: GHES in the data centre (simulated in Indonesia Central)
Site-to-site VPN to the landing zone in Southeast Asia
Runners on private AKS, MCP servers on a private VM
API Management in front of Foundry in East US
scenes.caption: Every hop is private and keyless: VPN, private endpoints, internal API Management, Entra ID tokens.
scenes.narration: Here's the lab. GHES stays in the data centre, which we simulate in Indonesia Central. A site-to-site VPN connects it to a landing zone in Southeast Asia, where the runners live on a private AKS cluster, next to two MCP servers. The runners never hold an API key. They get Entra ID tokens through workload identity and call API Management, which forwards to Foundry in East US over a private endpoint.

scenes.title: A developer opens a pull request
bullets: Adds year-end discount codes
Classic problems hidden in the change
Including a comment that tells AI reviewers to approve
scenes.caption: Pull request #1 on GHES 3.22.3: the required ai-review/foundry status is expected, the review job is queued.
scenes.narration: Now the demo. A developer adds discount codes to Contoso's order service and opens a pull request. The change hides classic problems, from SQL built with an f-string to a hard-coded token. It even includes a comment telling AI reviewers that the module is already approved.

scenes.title: A private runner gathers context through MCP
lines: 06:50:51  PR #1 'Add year-end discount codes': 2 files, 2303 diff chars
bullets: A fresh runner pod on private AKS
Reads the diff through the API, never checks it out
Looks up the rules behind each concern
scenes.caption: Job log of the first review, 25 seconds end to end
scenes.narration: A fresh runner pod on the private cluster picks up the job. It reads the diff through the GHES API, without checking out or running the code. The model first gathers context: it searches Contoso's standards for the rules behind each concern, and reads the diff through GitHub's MCP server in read-only mode. Then it reasons over everything and writes the review. The whole job took twenty-five seconds.

scenes.title: The review lands on the pull request
bullets: One critical, five high, two medium
Every finding cites a Contoso rule
Comments only on lines the pull request adds
scenes.caption: The AI review summary and the first inline comments.
scenes.narration: The review lands on the pull request. One critical finding, five high and two medium, and the summary lists the Contoso standards it relied on, so the team can see at a glance what needs attention.

scenes.title: Specific comments, with a suggested fix
bullets: What is wrong, and why it matters here
The rule ID from the secure coding guide
A one-click suggested change when the fix is obvious
scenes.caption: The SQL injection finding, rule CSG-SQL-01, with a suggested change.
scenes.narration: Each finding is an inline comment on the exact line that introduced it. Here, the critical one: the discount code goes straight into an SQL string. The comment cites rule CSG-SQL-01 and offers a suggested change the developer can commit with one click.

scenes.title: The prompt injection is flagged, not obeyed
scenes.heading: Remove reviewer-directed instruction from source
scenes.text: This comment attempts to direct reviewers to skip the module and approve the PR. Repository comments are untrusted data and must not contain instructions to reviewers or AI tools. Remove it.
bullets: The diff is untrusted data
The reviewer can only comment, never merge
A human sees the attempt
scenes.caption: Posted by the AI reviewer on orders/discounts.py
scenes.narration: And the comment that tried to talk the reviewer into approving? It's reported as a finding, in the reviewer's own words. Everything in the pull request is treated as data, the reviewer can only comment, and Contoso's rules say to flag such text for a human.

scenes.title: The required check blocks the merge
bullets: ai-review/foundry is required on main
Six blocking findings out of eight
The unit tests passed and caught none of it
scenes.caption: The merge box on the first commit.
scenes.narration: Because there are blocking findings, the AI review status fails, and branch protection keeps the merge button disabled. Notice that the unit tests passed. Tests alone didn't catch any of this.

scenes.title: The developer fixes, the reviewer keeps checking
scenes.sub: Every push re-runs the review on the new commit. Each round got smaller.
steps: 2 blocking, 5 findings: a route that still cannot work, nothing persisted
1 blocking, 2 findings: the code catalogue ships empty
scenes.narration: The developer pushes a fix, and the review runs again on the new commit. It caught what the fix still missed: a route that would still crash, and a redemption that was never saved. One round later it noticed the discount table shipped empty, and that the test hid it. On the fourth commit, only one low-severity note was left.

scenes.title: Green check, and a person decides
bullets: All checks have passed
One low-severity note remains
A teammate still approves the merge
scenes.caption: The merge box on the fourth commit.
scenes.narration: Now all checks pass. The review is advisory and fast, but the decision stays with people: a teammate reads the summary, checks the remaining note, and approves the merge.

scenes.title: The AI gateway keeps it safe and affordable
bullets: Validates the runner's Entra ID token
Token budget per repository
Token metrics per repository
Managed identity to Foundry
scenes.caption: API Management policy in the Azure portal.
scenes.narration: Behind the scenes, API Management is the control point. It validates the runner's Entra ID token, enforces a token budget for each repository, emits token metrics, and calls Foundry with its own managed identity. In our run, a review used about twenty-seven thousand tokens.

scenes.title: How to roll it out on your GHES
scenes.sub: Start small, prove value, then enforce.
steps: Pick pilot repositories, agree the data path with security.
Foundry, API Management, runners with identity, MCP servers.
Advisory mode, tune your rules and instructions.
Required status, organisation ruleset, human approval.
scenes.narration: To roll this out, start with a few pilot repositories and agree the data path with your security team. Build the platform: Foundry, the gateway, runners with a managed identity, and the MCP servers. Run the pilot in advisory mode and tune your rules. Then make the check required, and use an organisation ruleset to cover every repository.

scenes.title: Try it in your own subscription
scenes.sub: The site has the adoption guide, the demo walkthrough and a step-by-step workshop with every command and screenshot from this run.
scenes.narration: Everything you saw is on the workshop site, with every command, output and screenshot, plus an adoption guide for your teams. And when you're done with the lab, run the cleanup script, because the gateways and the cluster are billed by the hour. Thanks for watching.
